text: Johnson begins from a plain distrust of contemporary praise. The admiration a poet wins in his own lifetime may come from fashion or from the favour of a party, and neither can be relied upon to tell what is good. What can be relied upon is length of esteem. A work that has been read by men who shared none of its first readers' habits, and who had no reason to flatter its author, has been tried by many minds and kept; such a trial is the nearest thing criticism has to proof. Shakespeare, by Johnson's reckoning, had already stood it. He had outlived every rival and every patron, and the customs and allusions that once gave his scenes their local savour had grown obscure. The taste of the stage had altered more than once in a century and a half, and the learned had found fault with his irregularities. He was still read and still acted, by people who knew nothing of the quarrels of his own day. Johnson put the matter in a single figure (Johnson 1765): "The stream of time, which is continually washing the dissoluble fabricks of other poets, passes without injury by the adamant of Shakespeare."
